title: The Map Precedes the Territory: Reims, Nanterre, the Desert, and the Rue Sainte-Beuve
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Reims: The First of the Family to Study

stops.name: Reims, the birth in the champagne country
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, day of month contested. Wikipedia and the criticalsecret.com chronology give 27 July 1929 at Reims; per the background dossier, Le Monde's obituary gives 20 July and the Guardian's 29 July, neither of which could be fetched directly, so that spread is relayed rather than confirmed. Coordinate is Reims city centre; the birth address is not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: In Reims, in the cathedral city of the chalk country, a son is born to a gendarme and, by one account, a postal worker: Ardennais peasants one generation into the civil service. The house keeps no library and no learned tradition. What it keeps is the discipline of small state employment, the uniform, the hours, the forms filled in correctly. He will be the first of the family to enter a university, and he will describe that entry, much later, as a distance opening between himself and his parents. The sources cannot even agree which July day it was: the twentieth, the twenty-seventh, the twenty-ninth. No one has settled it since.
suggested_refs: The Le Monde and Guardian obituaries of March 2007, which give conflicting birth dates

stops.name: Reims, the lycee and the science of imaginary solutions
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The Peillet link is reported by Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy without a primary document, and neither names the school building, so the coordinate is Reims city centre rather than a landmark. The date orders the segment within his lycee years; no year is given by any source.
stops.campa: He goes through the lycee at Reims on a scholarship, a provincial boy on the state's money, and a philosophy teacher named Emmanuel Peillet puts Alfred Jarry in front of him. Pataphysics: the science of imaginary solutions, the study of the laws governing exceptions, a joke carried through with total gravity. It is the first system he meets that treats the absurd as a method rather than as a failure of method. Nothing in the record names the building, the year, or the other pupils in the room, only the teacher and the book he put across the desk.
suggested_refs: Alfred Jarry, Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien (1911)

stops.name: Paris, hypokhagne on the rue Clovis
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the criticalsecret.com chronology gives 1948 for the Henri-IV hypokhagne; the month is a default. This is also the correction to a common error, since Wikipedia dates his diplome d'etudes superieures on Nietzsche and Luther to 1948, which is untenable, a DES being a post-licence degree; 1948 is the year of entry to Henri-IV, not the year of the degree. Coordinate is the school at 23 rue Clovis.
stops.campa: At nineteen he arrives on the rue Clovis, in the hypokhagne of the Lycee Henri-IV, on the track that runs to the Ecole normale superieure and from there into the whole apparatus of French intellectual authority. It is the road the republic keeps open for provincial scholarship boys, and he is walking it. Then he breaks it off. He leaves without the agregation and without the normalien's title, which is also to leave without the network that title distributes. No source consulted gives a reason. He will never hold a chair at the College de France.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Henri-IV, 23 rue Clovis, Paris 5e, and its hypokhagne registers

stops.name: Arles, the season laying stone
stops.date_confidence: Attested but thin: the criticalsecret.com chronology reports mason's work in the Arles region after he left the hypokhagne track, with some accounts adding agricultural labour. No worksite, village, or employer is named in any source consulted, so the coordinate stands for the region and not a site. The date is an ordering approximation.
stops.campa: Off the track, he goes south and works with his hands. In the country around Arles he is a mason, and by some accounts a field labourer, laying stone through a Provencal summer while the classmates he left on the rue Clovis prepare for the concours. It is the only stretch of his life spent in physical labour. The record holds nothing about it beyond the bare fact that it happened: no village, no worksite, no man who employed him, no date on which the season ends.
suggested_refs: The criticalsecret.com chronology of Baudrillard, the only source for the Arles interval

segments.name: German Letters, and the Tubingen Year

stops.name: La Sorbonne, Nietzsche against Luther
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to substance, uncertain as to year. Wikipedia dates the Nietzsche and Luther diplome d'etudes superieures to 1948, which cannot stand, since the DES follows the licence and 1948 is his Henri-IV entry. The degree belongs to the early 1950s, before the 1952 Tubingen lectorate; c. 1949-1952. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He comes back to Paris and takes up German: the language, the literature, the philosophy. He is training to be a schoolmaster, and he will teach German in French lycees for six years, or eight, or ten, the chronologies not agreeing. At the Sorbonne he writes a diplome d'etudes superieures on Nietzsche and Martin Luther, the ecstatic set against the reformer, the hammer against the ninety-five theses. The pairing sets a habit he never afterward breaks, of reading one thought against the thought that ought to annihilate it.
suggested_refs: The lost DES memoir on Nietzsche and Luther, unpublished and untraced

stops.name: Tubingen, the lectorate and the Holderlin nobody printed
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the criticalsecret.com chronology gives a Tubingen lectorate for 1952-1953 and reports an unpublished Holderlin translation made there. The Tubingen stay is independently confirmed; the translation is a specialist-chronology claim relayed through the dossier and has not been seen. Month is a default.
stops.campa: He crosses into West Germany as a lecteur at Tubingen, his first long residence outside France, in a country seven years out of the ruin. He is twenty-three, and what he carries out of Swabia is not a book but German itself, the language his entire first career is built on. Here he also translates Holderlin, who spent his last thirty-six years mad in a tower on the Neckar in this same town. The translation is never published. It survives, if it survives at all, as a single line in a chronology.
suggested_refs: The Holderlinturm on the Neckar at Tubingen

stops.name: Editions du Seuil, the reader's desk on the rue Jacob
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Seuil readership and the 1962-1963 criticism for Les Temps modernes are given by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the criticalsecret.com chronology. The start of his lycee German teaching is genuinely contradictory across sources, 1956 per SEP against 1960 in other chronologies, with only the 1966 endpoint agreed; flagged, not resolved. Coordinate is Seuil's historic address at 27 rue Jacob, approximated, as no source gives a street.
stops.campa: Between the lycee classroom and the university he sits at a publisher's desk, reading German and philosophy manuscripts for Editions du Seuil, and writing literary criticism for Les Temps modernes, Sartre's journal, in 1962 and 1963. He is past thirty and has published nothing under his own name that anyone will later cite. It is the ordinary Parisian apprenticeship: judge other men's books, review a few, wait. The chronologies cannot agree when the schoolteaching began, 1956 or 1958 or 1960, though all of them end it in 1966.
suggested_refs: Baudrillard's literary criticism in Les Temps modernes, 1962-1963

segments.name: Nanterre, and the System of Objects

stops.name: Nanterre, the jury of Lefebvre, Barthes and Bourdieu
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the criticalsecret.com chronology all give the 1966 Nanterre appointment under Henri Lefebvre and the Lefebvre, Barthes and Bourdieu jury; one archival source dates the thesis to September 1966. Sources vary on his exact rank, assistant against maitre de conferences. Coordinate is the corpus pin for the Nanterre campus.
stops.campa: The new campus at Nanterre stands on cleared ground beside a shantytown, concrete blocks raised for the overflow of the Sorbonne. Henri Lefebvre takes him on as an assistant in sociology, and there he defends his doctoral thesis, Le Systeme des objets, before a jury of Lefebvre, Roland Barthes and Pierre Bourdieu. Barthes had shown in Mythologies how a wrestling match or a plate of steak becomes a second-order sign. Baudrillard, who has sat in his seminar, takes the furniture itself, the sideboard, the automobile, the collection, and reads a whole domestic interior as a language.
suggested_refs: Roland Barthes, Mythologies (1957), the direct precursor of Baudrillard's sign-value

stops.name: Paris, Le Systeme des objets
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1968 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia. Month and day are defaults. Coordinate is the corpus canonical pin for central Paris; no publication venue is specified in the sources.
stops.campa: The thesis becomes his first book, and it goes through the modern interior room by room. The sideboard that used to hold a family's authority and now holds nothing. The modular furniture that can be arranged any way and therefore means nothing in particular. The collection whose last object is always the one missing. The car. The advertisement. Objects, he argues, no longer serve; they signify, and what they signify is each other. It is a young man's book written in the borrowed vocabulary of the linguists, and it sells slowly.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, Le Systeme des objets (Gallimard, 1968)

stops.name: Nanterre, the campus in May
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he was teaching at Nanterre through May 1968 and took part in the surrounding political and intellectual ferment (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy); no source consulted gives him a leadership role, an arrest, an injury, or a movement membership. The claim that he co-founded the Association populaire franco-chinoise with Guattari in 1962 is dossier-only and unconfirmed, tagged [R].
stops.campa: The uprising starts on his campus. Nanterre is closed at the beginning of May and the trouble moves to the Latin Quarter within days; by the end of the month ten million French workers are out. He is on the faculty through all of it, in the middle of the ferment, and no source consulted gives him a role in it: no arrest, no injury, no membership, no committee. Felix Guattari, who by one unconfirmed account had founded a Franco-Chinese association with him six years before, is here in the March 22 Movement. What Baudrillard did in those weeks the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The March 22 Movement at Nanterre, February to May 1968

stops.name: Paris, La Societe de consommation
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1970 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. The summary of the argument is a standard paraphrase and no passage is quoted; the remark about student readers is general characterization and not sourced to a reception study.
stops.campa: The second book takes the argument out of the apartment and into the whole economy. Consumption is not the satisfaction of needs, he writes, but the manufacture of them; the drugstore, the shopping centre, the tanned body, the packaged holiday form a system of differences by which people are sorted into ranks. The book comes out two years after the barricades, into a country that had just been told the opposite by everyone. Abundance is the new scarcity, and it is distributed unequally by design. Growth produces poverty at the same rate it produces goods.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, La Societe de consommation (1970)

stops.name: Nanterre, Martine Dupuis
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia gives the meeting as 1970 at Nanterre and the marriage as 1994, with a minority of notices giving 1995. Month and day are ordering defaults. The ages follow arithmetically from the stated dates. Coordinate is the corpus pin for the Nanterre campus.
stops.campa: At Nanterre he meets Martine Dupuis, called Marine. She is twenty-five; he is forty-one. Most of the private life is hers to tell, and most of it she has not told. They will not share a house for roughly twenty years, and they marry in 1994, twenty-four years after this. She becomes the keeper of his last decade and of everything that follows it: the witness at the illness, the donor of the archive, the source for a good half of what is known about how he actually lived.
suggested_refs: The 2016 interview with Marine Baudrillard at intertheory.org, conducted in the rue Sainte-Beuve apartment

stops.name: Aspen, the first crossing to America
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and place: Wikipedia and the criticalsecret.com chronology both give 1970, Aspen, Colorado, as his first recorded United States trip. Month and day are defaults. The description of Aspen as a festival town built on a silver boom is background and is not sourced to any Baudrillard document.
stops.campa: His first recorded crossing to the United States puts him in Aspen, Colorado, at eight thousand feet, in a played-out silver town that had remade itself into a festival of ideas for executives and physicists. He is forty-one and has never seen the country whose objects, advertisements and drugstores he has just spent two books analysing from a desk in Paris. It will take him fifteen more years to write America, and this is where the writing starts. Nothing survives of what he did in Aspen, or whom he spoke to, or how long he stayed.
suggested_refs: The Aspen Institute and the Aspen design conferences of the 1960s and 1970s

stops.name: Paris, the political economy of the sign
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1972 for Pour une critique de l'economie politique du signe per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia. Month and day are defaults. The exposition of sign-value is a standard paraphrase; no passage is quoted.
stops.campa: He gives the thing its name: sign-value. Beside use-value and exchange-value, the two Marx worked with, he sets a third, the value an object carries purely as a mark of difference, and he argues that in a consumer economy it is the one that governs. A washing machine works; it can be sold; and it says who you are. The third function has swallowed the first two. Marx had no place to put it. The book is the hinge of his whole career, and it is the last one he writes from inside political economy, in its vocabulary and its form.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, Pour une critique de l'economie politique du signe (1972)

stops.name: Paris, Le Miroir de la production
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1973 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. The account of the argument is a standard paraphrase. The claim about the cost to his standing on the French left is general characterization and is not sourced to a documented survey of reception.
stops.campa: He turns and fires on his own side. Marxism, he argues, is not the critique of capitalism but its mirror. It accepts production as the truth of the human, labour as the human essence, and history as the unfolding of both, which are capitalism's own premises restated with the sign reversed. The book costs him the French left, which had been his readership, and buys him nothing yet in exchange. To liberate the worker as a worker is to confirm the code that made him one.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, Le Miroir de la production (1973)

stops.name: Kyoto, the first crossing to Japan
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and city: Wikipedia's biographical timeline gives 1973, Kyoto. Month and day are defaults. The camera-gift dating is genuinely contradictory in the record, 1981 per Wikipedia's timeline against the late 1980s per Marine Baudrillard's recollection, and is left unresolved here; no source connects the camera to this first visit.
stops.campa: He goes to Japan for the first time, to Kyoto, and the country becomes a place he returns to across thirty years. What he did in Kyoto in 1973, whom he saw, what he was brought there to do, is not recorded in anything reachable: the trip is a date and the name of a city. Japan will eventually give him his first camera. When? Wikipedia's timeline puts the gift in 1981, his widow remembered it happening in the late eighties, and no source ties it to this visit at all.
suggested_refs: The 2016 Marine Baudrillard interview, which redates the camera to the late 1980s

stops.name: La Jolla, the first American university
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the criticalsecret.com chronology gives January to April 1975 at the University of California, San Diego, as his first extended United States university stay; the day is a default. The description of the campus is background. The list of later visiting posts is drawn from the same chronology and from Wikipedia.
stops.campa: From January to April he holds his first extended American university post, at the University of California, San Diego, on the bluffs above the Pacific at La Jolla. Eucalyptus, poured concrete, ocean fog, a campus raised in the nineteen-sixties on a mesa that had been marine-corps ground. He is teaching in the country whose ordinary surfaces are becoming his subject, and doing it in the state that manufactures most of them. The visiting appointments will keep arriving for twenty-five years: Santa Barbara, Irvine, Columbia, Montana.
suggested_refs: The University of California, San Diego, visiting appointment records for 1975

stops.name: Paris, L'Echange symbolique et la mort
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1976 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. Bataille's influence on the book is documented in the secondary literature and relayed here through the interlock lens rather than re-fetched. The quote comes from Forget Foucault (1977), a year later, and is given because reversibility is this book's governing term; the wording follows the 2007 Semiotext(e) body text, not the shorter form circulating from Lotringer's introduction.
stops.campa: The central book, and the hardest. Against production he sets symbolic exchange: the gift, the challenge, the duel, the potlatch, forms in which value is not accumulated but returned and cancelled. Death, in such a system, is not the end of a life but a term in a cycle that answers back. Modern society abolishes death by administering it, and pays for the abolition with a world in which nothing can be answered at all. Georges Bataille, on expenditure and sacrifice, stands directly behind the argument. Here too the orders of simulacra first appear: counterfeit, production, simulation.
stops.quote: Everything linear, including history, has an end; challenge alone is without end since it is indefinitely reversible. And it is this reversibility which gives it its prodigious force.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, Forget Foucault, trans. Nicole Dufresne (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents, 2007 edition), body text at c. p.61
suggested_refs: Georges Bataille, La Part maudite (1949), on expenditure and sovereignty

stops.name: Paris, Oublier Foucault
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the 1977 publication (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Wikipedia); month and day are defaults. The Forget Baudrillard riposte is tagged [R]: it is circulated intellectual folklore and no primary Foucault text containing the line has been located. The summary of Foucault's own position is background. Quote verified in the archive.org scan of the Semiotext(e) Foreign Agents volume.
stops.campa: Michel Foucault had spent a decade building an analytics of power: capillary, productive, everywhere at once. Baudrillard publishes a hundred pages arguing that the account works too well, that a discourse able to describe power that exhaustively is describing something already finished, and that Foucault writes with such clarity because his object has evaporated under him. The title is an instruction. No Foucault text has ever been produced containing the reply that gets repeated in every account of the quarrel: that the correct title would be Forget Baudrillard.
stops.quote: Power is no more held than a secret is extracted, for the secrecy of power is the same as that of the secret: it does not exist.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, Forget Foucault (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents), p.58
suggested_refs: Michel Foucault, La Volonte de savoir (1976), the immediate target of the polemic

stops.name: Beaubourg, the effect of the new museum
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to sourcing. Both L'Effet Beaubourg (1977) and the Traverses connection come from the background dossier and were not independently re-fetched this pass, though both are well attested in the general secondary literature. The Centre Pompidou opened on 31 January 1977; the month here is an ordering default.
stops.campa: The Centre Georges Pompidou opens in the Beaubourg quarter with its guts on the outside, pipes and ducts and escalators in primary colours bolted to the facade, and the crowds arrive in numbers nobody had planned for. He writes L'Effet Beaubourg and calls the thing a machine for the implosion of culture: a structure built to circulate the masses through art at speed, whose real content is the circulation. Around the same time he helps found Traverses, a journal produced out of the Centre's own industrial-design wing.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, L'Effet Beaubourg: implosion et dissuasion (Galilee, 1977)

stops.name: Paris, De la seduction
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the 1979 publication and for the feminist criticism the book drew (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Wikipedia); month and day are defaults. The quote is from Forget Foucault (1977), not from Seduction itself, and the source line says so.
stops.campa: Against production he now sets seduction, and against liberation, reversibility. Seduction is not sex and not persuasion; it is the play of appearances, the sign that turns back on itself, the strategy of the weaker term that wins by disappearing. He writes that the feminine has never been the opposite of the masculine but its seduction, and the argument draws hard feminist criticism, then and since, for making a metaphysical figure out of women. He does not withdraw it.
stops.quote: Seduction is stronger than production. It is stronger than sexuality and must never be confused with it.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, Forget Foucault (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents), p.55
suggested_refs: Jane Gallop and other feminist responses to De la seduction, 1980s

stops.name: Paris, Simulacres et simulation
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication 1981 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. The Borges fable is 'On Exactitude in Science'; Baudrillard's reversal of it opens the book, a documented literary borrowing. The quote is from Forget Foucault (1977), given for the formulation, and is not from this book.
stops.campa: The book opens on a borrowed fable. Jorge Luis Borges tells of an empire whose cartographers drew a map so exact it covered the territory point for point, and which rotted afterwards in the deserts along with the empire. Baudrillard turns it over: today the map precedes the territory, and it is the real that rots. He runs the thesis through Disneyland, which exists to make the rest of America look real; through Watergate, a scandal staged to prove scandal is still possible; through nuclear deterrence, a war held permanently in the condition of not happening.
stops.quote: All things come to an end in their redoubled simulation — a sign that a cycle is completed.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, Forget Foucault (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents), p.57
suggested_refs: Jorge Luis Borges, 'Del rigor en la ciencia' (1946), the fable of the map coextensive with the empire

stops.name: New York, the book that has no French original
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Internet Archive catalogue record for Simulations (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents, New York, 1983, ISBN 0936756020) confirms the volume, and it is well documented that no French book of that title exists. Month and day are defaults. Coordinate is Columbia University, where Semiotext(e) was based and where Baudrillard later held a professor-level connection per IMEC via his Radical Philosophy obituary; the exact appointment dates and status are not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Sylvere Lotringer, running Semiotext(e) out of Columbia University, assembles a slim black paperback called Simulations and puts it into American art schools, English departments and downtown bookshops. There is no French book of that title. It is a compilation, cut out of several volumes and translated into one, and for a decade it is what English readers mean when they say Baudrillard. The American Baudrillard is an editorial construction before he is a translated author: Simulacra and Simulation does not appear whole in English until 1994.
suggested_refs: Simulations (Semiotext(e), Foreign Agents, New York, 1983), archive.org/details/simulations0000baud

stops.name: Sydney, the evil demon of images
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and country: the criticalsecret.com chronology lists 1984 Australia, corroborating the dossier and permitting an upgrade from the [R] the research pool gave it. The Power Institute lecture series and the 1987 publication of The Evil Demon of Images are dossier claims that could not be independently re-fetched. Month is a default. Coordinate corrected to the University of Sydney main campus; the value carried in the research pool had a sign error and fell in the North Pacific.
stops.campa: His first recorded visit to Australia takes him to the Power Institute at the University of Sydney, where he lectures on the image. The chronology records a year and a country, and what he did in Sydney does not survive. The lectures do: they become The Evil Demon of Images, published there in 1987, with Descartes's deceiving demon moved off the senses and onto the screen. The images no longer deceive by lying about the real, which is the whole of the old complaint against pictures. They produce it.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, The Evil Demon of Images (Power Institute, Sydney, 1987)

stops.name: Santa Barbara, the campus and the driving
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the UCSB stay in 1985 (criticalsecret.com chronology); month and day are defaults. The road-trip material is attested through America itself, published 1986, but the itinerary is nowhere documented stop by stop, so the account of what he saw follows the book rather than a travel record.
stops.campa: A stay at the University of California, Santa Barbara, on the lagoon at Goleta, and around it the driving. He crosses the country by road: interstates, motels, salt flats, parking lots the size of villages, joggers, television sets left burning in empty rooms. He is not conducting fieldwork and refuses the word for it. He is looking for the place where a theory and a desert turn out to be the same shape. The notebooks from these months become Amerique.
suggested_refs: The University of California, Santa Barbara, visiting appointment records for 1985

stops.name: Las Vegas, neon in daylight
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Las Vegas is among the cities he photographed: the Chateau Shatto exhibition listing dates his prints 1985-2003 and names Venice, Paris, Amsterdam, Rio, Las Vegas and Bruges. The exact year and month of any visit are not established and this date orders the segment. A source error in the research pool is corrected here: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry does not mention Las Vegas, America, or an American road trip, and that citation is withdrawn.
stops.campa: Neon burning in daylight, a city of signs standing in the Mojave with nothing at all behind them, and he photographs it. Las Vegas is the American proof of his case: not a false city pretending to be real, but a real city built entirely out of the false, and prospering on the arrangement. The desert around it he treats as the true American landscape, the ground the cities are laid on. He keeps coming back with a camera. Prints made in Las Vegas will hang in the posthumous exhibitions, beside Venice, Amsterdam, Rio and Bruges.
suggested_refs: Chateau Shatto, 'Ultimate Paradox: The Photography of Jean Baudrillard', Los Angeles, 2015-2016

stops.name: Paris, Amerique
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1986 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. The paraphrase of the book's positions is standard. The characterization of French reviewers is general and is not sourced to a documented survey of reception.
stops.campa: Amerique appears: a theoretical travelogue with no argument in the ordinary sense, written in the register of a man driving and looking. America, he says, is utopia achieved, which is exactly why it cannot be forgiven; the desert is its truth and the freeway its liturgy; the country lives out the ideas Europe only thinks. French reviewers accuse him of tourism, and he does not answer them. He is not describing a nation and has never said that he was.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, Amerique (Grasset, 1986)

segments.name: The Events That Did Not Take Place

stops.name: Porte Dauphine, leaving Nanterre
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with a correction to the research pool. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's 'retired from Nanterre in 1987' is compressed and misstates what happened. French Wikipedia gives him as scientific director at Paris-IX Dauphine 1986-1990, English Wikipedia gives the move to IRIS at Dauphine in 1986, and the criticalsecret.com chronology gives habilitation in 1986, four years at Dauphine, and 1990 as his permanent exit from the university. Month is a default. Coordinate is the Dauphine campus at Porte Dauphine, supplied here rather than taken from a source.
stops.campa: He leaves Nanterre after twenty years, and not by retirement: it is a transfer. He becomes scientific director at the Institut de recherche et d'information socio-economique at Paris-IX Dauphine, in the old NATO headquarters at the Porte Dauphine, and habilitates the same year. Four years later he leaves the university altogether, at sixty-one. He never holds a French chair again, and from here the work goes out through newspapers and foreign lecture halls.
suggested_refs: The Institut de recherche et d'information socio-economique, Universite Paris-IX Dauphine

stops.name: Paris, the war that did not take place
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy date the essays and their collection to 1991; the dossier gives the three Liberation dates as 4 January, 6 February and 29 March 1991, and the last of these is used as the anchor. The quote was seen page-cited inside a secondary scholarly essay at pomoculture.org and not in the primary volume, whose archive.org PDF returned 404.
stops.campa: Three essays in Liberation around the Gulf War, the last of them four days after the ceasefire, and a title that will follow him into the grave: the Gulf War did not take place. He does not mean that nobody died, and he says so. He means that a campaign flown from the air by one side against a force it outmatched absolutely, watched by the world as green footage, lacks the reciprocity and the risk that make a war a war. The misreading outruns the argument at once and never stops. Christopher Norris answers him with a whole book.
stops.quote: We are no longer in a logic of the passage from virtual to actual but in a hyperrealist logic of the deterrence of the real by the virtual.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, The Gulf War Did Not Take Place, trans. Paul Patton (Indiana University Press, 1995), p.27
suggested_refs: Christopher Norris, Uncritical Theory: Postmodernism, Intellectuals and the Gulf War (1992)
sources: pomoculture.org, secondary essay quoting Patton's translation

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the southern tour
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the weakest-evidenced stop in the file. The 1991 Latin American tour through Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela, Colombia and Chile is a dossier claim only; no source consulted names an Argentine city, and Buenos Aires is a placement rather than a documented venue. An independent check was attempted and the session's search budget ran out before the query executed. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Buenos Aires pin. Month is an ordering default.
stops.campa: A lecture tour of Latin America: Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela, Colombia, Chile. In Buenos Aires he speaks in the city of the man whose one-paragraph fable about a map opened his most famous book, ten years after that book. This is the thinnest stop in his itinerary: the dossier names five countries and not one street, and the attempt to confirm it independently ran out of budget before the query went out. Did he mention Borges from the platform? No source consulted says where he lectured, or who came, or whether the name was spoken at all.

stops.name: Paris, L'Illusion de la fin
stops.date_confidence: Attested: publication year 1992 per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. The paraphrase of the argument is standard. The quote is the epigraph of The Gulf War Did Not Take Place, seen quoted in a secondary essay with the ellipsis already in place, and it is given here because the two books argue the same case; it is not from L'Illusion de la fin.
stops.campa: The Berlin Wall is three years down, the Soviet Union a year gone, and the historians are announcing the end of history. He argues the opposite, and worse: history has not ended, it has stopped, and then gone into reverse. Events no longer accumulate toward anything. They are recycled, commemorated, rerun, apologised for, and a century spends its last decade digesting itself in public, and the commemorations fill the space where a direction of travel used to be. Progress has not been defeated by anybody. It has simply stopped going anywhere.
stops.quote: Since this war was won in advance, we will never know what it would have been like had it existed...
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, The Gulf War Did Not Take Place, trans. Paul Patton (Indiana University Press, 1995), used as epigraph
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, L'Illusion de la fin, ou la greve des evenements (Galilee, 1992)
sources: pomoculture.org, secondary essay quoting the epigraph

stops.name: Paris, no pity for Sarajevo
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the essay ran in Liberation on 8 January 1994. Two published English translations exist and differ materially, Chris Turner's in The Perfect Crime (Verso, 1996) and James Petterson's in This Time We Knew (NYU Press, 1996, p.80); the Turner wording is used. A correction to the research pool: its wording matched no published translation and its Aperture citation could not be substantiated, so both are withdrawn.
stops.campa: Sarajevo is in its twenty-first month under siege. Baudrillard publishes Pas de pitie pour Sarajevo in Liberation and attacks not the siege but the pity: the Western intellectual who travels to a dying city in order to recover, out of other people's reality, a reality he has mislaid at home. They are the strong ones, he writes, and we are the weak. The piece is read widely as cynicism delivered from an armchair in the sixth arrondissement. He never claims to have gone to Bosnia. He is writing about the ones who did.
stops.quote: It is they who are the strong ones and we who are weak, going over there looking for the means to make up for our weakness and loss of reality.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, 'No Pity for Sarajevo,' in The Perfect Crime, trans. Chris Turner (Verso, 1996)
suggested_refs: Thomas Cushman and Stjepan Mestrovic, eds., This Time We Knew: Western Responses to Genocide in Bosnia (NYU Press, 1996), which prints a rival translation
sources: Jean Baudrillard, 'Pas de pitie pour Sarajevo,' Liberation, 8 January 1994
The Perfect Crime, trans. Chris Turner (Verso, 1996)

stops.name: Rue Sainte-Beuve, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1994 (Wikipedia and most specialist chronologies), with a minority of notices giving 1995; unresolved. Month and day are defaults. Coordinate is the rue Sainte-Beuve address named in the Marine Baudrillard interview at intertheory.org. The research pool carried two coordinates roughly 200 m apart for this same address; the afterlife value is used here and again at the death, so the file is internally consistent.
stops.campa: Twenty-four years after Nanterre, they marry. He is sixty-four and she is forty-nine, and they have been in one another's lives since she was a student on that campus. The apartment is on the rue Sainte-Beuve in the sixth arrondissement, a short street off the boulevard Raspail named after a critic. Some notices give the year as 1995 instead. Marine Baudrillard will spend the next three decades as custodian of the work: the archive, the library, the photographs, and the interviews that supply the biography he declined to write.
suggested_refs: The rue Sainte-Beuve apartment, Paris 6e, where the 2016 interview with Marine Baudrillard was conducted

segments.name: The Camera and the Late Lectures

stops.name: Karlsruhe, the Siemens Media Art Prize
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the prize and the year: zkm.de carries a page titled 'Siemens-Medienkunstpreis 1995: Jean Baudrillard'. That page gives no ceremony date, so month and day are defaults. Coordinate corrected to ZKM's actual site at Lorenzstrasse 19 in the former IWKA munitions works; the research pool carried two different and both incorrect values for this one institution.
stops.campa: The Zentrum fur Kunst und Medien at Karlsruhe, installed in a disused munitions works by the railway, gives him the Siemens Media Art Prize. The prize page the institution still keeps carries a title and a photograph and nothing else: no ceremony date, no citation, no speech. It is an art institution honouring a sociologist, and it marks where his readership has gone, out of the sociology departments that never quite claimed him and into the museums, the media-art programmes, the schools where people make images for a living.

stops.name: Paris, Ecran total
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the 1997 publication and for the quoted line, both by way of the Radical Philosophy obituary; month and day are defaults. The Liberation column run is directly contradictory across sources: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives June 1987 to May 1997, other chronologies give a single year from June 1995. Both cannot be right and the conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: He publishes Ecran total, a collection out of the newspaper years, and in it writes about AIDS and homosexuality in terms his obituarists were still flinching at ten years later. He does not soften the line and he never withdraws it. It belongs in the account beside the Gulf War essays and the Sarajevo piece: a writer who took reversibility for a law and applied it to the dying. The chronologies cannot even agree how long the Liberation column ran, ten years or one.
stops.quote: Those who live by the same shall perish by the same.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, Ecran total (1997), quoted in his Radical Philosophy obituary
suggested_refs: The Liberation columns, whose run is dated 1987-1997 by one chronology and 1995-1996 by another

stops.name: Irvine, the Wellek Library Lectures
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the dates 24, 25 and 27 May 1999 and the three lecture titles come from the UC Irvine Libraries' Wellek Library Lectures page. The Matrix opened on 31 March 1999; the hollowed-book detail, the Wachowskis' acknowledgement, and Baudrillard's own public rejection of the reading are attested via Wikipedia. The quote was seen in the Radical Philosophy obituary with book attribution and not in the primary lecture text.
stops.campa: Three lectures at the Critical Theory Institute of the University of California, Irvine, on the twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth and twenty-seventh of May: The Murder of the Real; The Final Solution: Cloning Beyond the Human and the Inhuman; The Millennium, or The Suspense of the Year 2000. Two months earlier a film had opened in which a character hides his contraband inside a hollowed-out copy of Simulacra and Simulation, and its directors had named him as an influence. He rejects the reading, publicly and more than once. The three lectures become The Vital Illusion.
stops.quote: Everything will be preceded by its virtual realization... This pure, absolute reality, this unconditional realization of the world, this is what I call the Perfect Crime.
stops.quote_source: Jean Baudrillard, The Vital Illusion (2000), quoted in his Radical Philosophy obituary
suggested_refs: lib.uci.edu, Wellek Library Lectures: Jean Baudrillard, May 1999

stops.name: Paris, the photographs at the Maison Europeenne
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the venue and the run, which Wikipedia gives across 1999 and 2000; month and day are defaults. The camera-gift dating remains contradictory, 1981 per Wikipedia's timeline against the late 1980s per Marine Baudrillard, and is not resolved. His refusal to have the photographs read as illustrations of the theory is a general characterization from the dossier and is not a quoted statement.
stops.campa: His photographs go up at the Maison europeenne de la photographie in the Marais: colour, saturated, mostly emptied of people, surfaces caught at the angle where they stop being surfaces. He insists the pictures are not illustrations of the theory and refuses to let them be read that way. He has been shooting since the eighties with a camera given to him in Japan, and the giving is dated to 1981 by one source and to the late eighties by his wife. The exhibition runs across 1999 and 2000.
suggested_refs: The Maison europeenne de la photographie exhibition of Baudrillard's photographs, 1999-2000

stops.name: Saas-Fee, the school under the glacier
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the European Graduate School affiliation and for the surviving video record (English Wikipedia and the European Graduate School biography page, pact.egs.edu). The precise start year is not established in any source consulted, and this date orders the segment. The description of the village is background.
stops.campa: In the Saastal, at eighteen hundred metres, under the Fee glacier, in a car-free village that fills and empties with the skiing season, the European Graduate School runs a summer programme in philosophy and media. He teaches there from the school's early years until his death, in a division named for the philosophy of culture and media criticism. The lectures are filmed, and more of him survives on video out of this alpine village than out of thirty years of French lecture halls. No source consulted names the year he began.
suggested_refs: The European Graduate School video archive of Baudrillard's Saas-Fee lectures

segments.name: The Absolute Event, and the Rue Sainte-Beuve

stops.name: Paris, L'Esprit du terrorisme
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with the date corrected. French Wikipedia gives the Le Monde publication as 3 November 2001; 2 November also circulates, and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy carries it, because Le Monde's printed issue bears a cover date one day ahead of newsstand appearance. The printed issue date is the citable one. The account of the argument follows the essay's own terms; the essay claims no foreknowledge and offers no moral endorsement.
stops.campa: Eight weeks after the towers, Le Monde prints his essay on them. He calls it the absolute event, the mother of events, the one that had absorbed all the events that never happened. And he writes that the West did not only fear the strike but wished it, that the condemnation and the forbidden jubilation were both real and both present in the same people. He is accused of justifying murder. The essay claims no foreknowledge and endorses nothing. What it says is that a hegemony provokes the desire for its own destruction, including among those who live off it.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, 'L'Esprit du terrorisme,' Le Monde, 3 November 2001

stops.name: Karlsruhe, Baudrillard und die Kunste
stops.date_confidence: Attested that a 'Baudrillard and the Arts' conference was held in his honour at ZKM Karlsruhe in 2004 around his seventy-fifth birthday (English Wikipedia); the precise dates of 16 to 18 July come from the dossier only and are not independently confirmed. Coordinate corrected as at the 1995 stop. The remark about the illness follows Marine Baudrillard's account, which places its onset around 2001, against Wikipedia's 2005 diagnosis date; the conflict is unresolved.
stops.campa: For his seventy-fifth birthday the ZKM mounts Jean Baudrillard und die Kunste: a symposium and an exhibition, his photographs on the walls, his papers in the cases, and the artists and theorists who had been reading him for twenty years in the room. Karlsruhe had given him the prize nine years earlier, in the same building by the railway, the same institution deciding a second time that he belonged to art rather than to sociology. He is seventy-five, some years into the illness on his wife's reckoning, and still travelling.
suggested_refs: ZKM Karlsruhe, 'Jean Baudrillard und die Kunste', July 2004
sources: background dossier for the July dates

stops.name: Madrid, the Gold Medal of the Circulo
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the award and the venue (circulobellasartes.com/en/medallas/jean-baudrillard/), which confirms the medal and a speech but carries no date; the 23 November 2005 date comes from the dossier only. The summary of the lecture follows the published title, Dominacion y hegemonia, and the volume La agonia del poder.
stops.campa: The Circulo de Bellas Artes on the calle de Alcala gives him its Gold Medal, the highest thing it has to give, and he speaks there on domination and hegemony. He is seventy-six and ill, and this is one of his last lectures, delivered in a language that is not his own. Domination, he argues, could be resisted, because it had a master and a subject and therefore a relation; hegemony has neither, and cannot be opposed, only aggravated. The talk becomes La agonia del poder.
suggested_refs: Jean Baudrillard, La agonia del poder (Circulo de Bellas Artes, Madrid)

stops.name: Rue Sainte-Beuve, the death at home
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the death: 6 March 2007, Paris 6e, per English and French Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, at his home on the rue Sainte-Beuve per the Marine Baudrillard interview. The diagnosis date is contradictory: Wikipedia gives 2005, while his widow dates the onset to around 2001 and describes a four-year illness; unresolved. The quote is tagged [R], quoted in the Radical Philosophy obituary without an originating text named.
stops.campa: He dies at home on the rue Sainte-Beuve, in the sixth arrondissement, at seventy-seven. His wife's account puts the beginning of the illness around 2001, straight after September, with treatment, then a spread into the nervous and circulatory systems, four years of it. Wikipedia dates the cancer diagnosis to 2005. The two accounts do not agree and nobody has reconciled them. The site of the cancer is not established in anything reachable, and the exact street number is not given in any source consulted.
stops.quote: Dying is pointless, you have to know how to disappear
stops.quote_source: attributed to Jean Baudrillard in his Radical Philosophy obituary, which does not name the originating book or essay
suggested_refs: The 2016 interview with Marine Baudrillard, intertheory.org/marinebaudrillard.htm

stops.name: Abbaye d'Ardenne, the papers that escaped him
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the IMEC press release gives 4 April 2016, Marine Baudrillard as donor, and the contents as corrected typescripts, notebooks, dossiers of preparatory notes, working files, editorial files, annotated books and iconographic and audiovisual material. The fonds page 787BDL carries the phrase about the destruction of traces verbatim. Baudrillard never visited the Abbaye d'Ardenne; this stop marks where his working papers physically are, not a journey he made. Coordinate corrected to 49.1964, -0.4139; the research pool carried two different wrong values. The Reid Hall library figures rest on the dossier alone, the Columbia Global Centers page having returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: Nine years after, in a thirteenth-century abbey outside Caen that already holds the papers of Foucault, Derrida and Althusser, his archive is deposited: corrected typescripts, notebooks, dossiers of preparatory notes, working files, editorial files, annotated books, photographs, recordings. Marine Baudrillard is the donor. The institute's own description says these are the archives that escaped his taste for the destruction of traces, which is how the story got about that he had burned everything. His annotated library, some fifteen hundred volumes, went separately to Reid Hall in Paris.
suggested_refs: IMEC fonds 787BDL, Abbaye d'Ardenne; the Jean Baudrillard Library at Columbia Global Centers Paris, Reid Hall
